Notes

A party call turns into contempt for online posturing, then the guest verses bring that distrust onto roads, into factories and through the family home.

麻痹

This riffs on the established internet catchphrase 睡你麻痹起来嗨, “fuck sleeping, get up and party,” circulating in 2015 memes and music remixes. 麻痹 supplies a sound-alike profanity rather than a medical reference to numbness. Adding 给我, “for me / do as I say,” turns the invitation into an order. It is a loudly social opening for a verse about living in one’s own little world.

  • Bilibili: 2015 remix of the get-up-and-party catchphrase
随意开卖

The pants and microphone make a tiny checklist for going out into the street, and 开卖 announces the start of selling. Performance is presented with the casual practicality of setting up a stall. The shift from “get wild” to “get ready to sell” puts play and livelihood beside one another, without pausing to make them separate identities.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
纸上谈兵

纸上谈兵 means discussing war on paper: theory or bravado without the practical ability to act. Jackzebra follows it with tantrums, an overloaded feed and diplomatic declarations. The idiom tells us what he thinks those actions lack—effective force outside words. Chun later picks up the same distinction by demanding confrontation beyond Moments and fan chats.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
朋友圈刷屏

刷屏 means filling a feed or screen with posts. It makes an outburst visible in volume even if it cannot make the person more powerful. The next lines supply official-sounding condemnation; later Chun mentions both Moments and fan groups. The song keeps distinguishing an audience for anger from an ability to act on it.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
强烈谴责

强烈谴责 and 严正抗议 are the official formulas “strongly condemn” and “solemnly protest,” familiar from diplomatic statements. Their placement after flooding a social feed inflates a personal quarrel to the scale of state affairs. Then “so what?” collapses the ceremony. The joke is in the register and its ineffective grandeur, not in identifying a particular diplomatic dispute.

  • Ministry of Foreign Affairs: diplomatic formula in use
骗鬼呢

骗鬼呢 literally asks whether someone is trying to fool ghosts, dismissing a claim as unbelievable. The supernatural language becomes a bridge into the final verse, where people themselves are hard to distinguish from ghosts. What begins as a casual comeback grows into a picture of social relations in which appearances cannot be trusted.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
城市套路多我回农村

Chun uses the familiar internet joke about escaping the city’s 套路, its elaborate tricks, by returning to the countryside. But his next line supplies potholes on the rural road. It denies an easy map with urban deception on one side and rural innocence on the other. The move changes the scenery without guaranteeing a less treacherous path.

  • Xinhua report on the circulated phrase, via People’s Daily
坑

坑 is both a hole in the ground and, colloquially, a trap, rip-off or bad deal. A muddy road makes the literal sense immediately visible; the preceding complaints about 套路 keep the social meaning active. The line is therefore a complete punchline in one image: even an escape from the city can land you in another kind of pit.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
人心隔肚皮

人心隔肚皮 says people’s hearts are hidden behind the belly’s skin: outward familiarity cannot make their intentions transparent. Chun immediately attaches online aggression to that opacity. The verse does not ask whether the screen persona is authentic because screens are inherently false; it starts from the more ordinary difficulty of knowing what any other person really wants.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
笨鸟先飞

笨鸟先飞 says the slower or less gifted bird should fly first—effort and an early start compensate for ability. Adding a body covered in shit ruins the proverb’s clean uplift. The bird may be working hard and still look filthy. A familiar lesson in self-improvement becomes an ungainly survivor, which fits the muddy road rather better than an inspirational success story.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
娘子

娘子 is an older address for a woman or wife, giving the plea a theatrical, old-fashioned courtesy. It is surrounded by money, excrement and threats, so the register briefly changes character. The verse keeps desire for a kiss close to desire for success. Romantic address does not soften the whole speaker; it is another voice he can reach for.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
跟我混

跟我混 means hanging around with, following or making one’s way under somebody’s lead. One line earlier money has the speaker trapped; now he offers himself as a route to it. The switch is comically abrupt. The verse can recognize money as a constraint and still reproduce the recruiting boast that promises an escape through the right connection.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
算命老师

老师 can respectfully address a skilled practitioner as well as a schoolteacher. Here the fortune-teller calls him, but later Chun insists that his progress came from no such master. 算命, calculating fate, is answered by 改命, changing it. The movement from receiving a prediction to claiming agency is one of the verse’s organizing contrasts.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
范冰冰

Fan Bingbing is the Chinese screen star. “My Fan Bingbing” makes celebrity beauty a personal comparison inside the verse’s repeated call for a woman’s attention. It belongs to the same expressive jump as 娘子: ordinary desire is briefly enlarged into a dramatic, glamorous scene, before speed, smoke and confrontation take over again.

  • San Sebastián Festival: Fan Bingbing biography
不是在朋友圈和粉丝群

Chun repeats Jackzebra’s distinction between talk and force but names the environments more precisely. 粉丝群 is a fan group chat, where an artist can rally an already sympathetic audience. Rejecting that arena questions how much courage it takes to perform confrontation among one’s own supporters. The claim is about where opposition happens as well as how loudly it is voiced.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
老子

老子 here is an aggressive first-person expression: the speaker magnifies himself through the authority of “your father / old man.” It is not the philosopher Laozi. The immediately surrounding regional phrasing gives the threat a direct spoken force that “I” alone would lose; English partly recovers that force through the profanity.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
好多人是鬼不能辨别

The final guest is 南部犯罪份子, the artist Jackzebra named as his favorite SoundCloud rapper in a 2025 Interview questionnaire. This entrance changes the song’s scale: generalized tricks give way to friendship, parents, factory work and recruitment fraud. Attribution matters here. The feature adds a distinct voice whose distrust takes shape through a different set of ordinary social encounters.

  • Interview: Jackzebra’s own listening and film picks
不听招呼

听招呼 in this regional usage is obeying instructions or behaving as told, not merely hearing a greeting. The threatened consequence is confinement. It sharply revises Jackzebra’s earlier claim that nobody can control you: in this guest’s scene, authority may have somewhere quite physical to put an uncooperative person.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
老汉

老汉 is “Dad” in regional speech here, paired with the preceding mother. The parents 拼命, expend themselves to the utmost, to send the child out toward a future. The later factory labor and crooked broker put that hope into jeopardy. Keeping the family terms ordinary matters: the verse’s social stakes come from a household’s effort, not an abstract statement about migration.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
天冷加衣天要亡你

The sentence begins with everyday care—wear something warmer—and turns instantly into a threat of annihilation. 天 does double work as weather in 天冷 and fate or heaven in 天要亡你. English has to change words to follow that turn. The same syllable moves from the world a parent helps you endure to a world that seems bent on destroying you.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
打着螺丝

打螺丝 is literally fastening screws and commonly stands for basic repetitive factory work. The ongoing 着 keeps the hands working while memory turns to friendship. This is a different image of the body from the excavator threats: it performs a small repeated task while the mind goes elsewhere. The following recruitment scam anchors that labor in a precarious route out of home.

  • People’s Daily: a factory worker’s account of starting with 打螺丝
黑中介

黑中介 is an illegitimate or unscrupulous intermediary. In this sequence—being sent out by parents, factory work, a rural newcomer—the relevant world is job placement. China’s labor ministry describes such brokers using false offers and inflated pay promises to take money from applicants. The lyric makes trust the point of entry: what is stolen first is the young man’s confidence in a connection.

  • Ministry of Human Resources: recruitment traps
眼中钉

眼中钉 is literally a nail in the eye: a person whose presence is intolerable and whom one wants removed. English “thorn in your side” carries the idiomatic meaning but changes the bodily violence. Coming after friendship mixed with interests and a cheated rural newcomer, the question asks how somebody can turn from a companion into an obstacle.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
吃人的人变成鬼

The verse’s ghosts are not safely separate monsters; exploitative people become them. After friendships mixed with interests and a fraudulent broker, “eating people” makes exploitation bodily and predatory. The repeated 鬼 has moved from Jackzebra’s sarcastic “fooling ghosts” to a social world in which a human face offers little assurance of human treatment.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
刀人

刀, “knife,” becomes a verb: to knife or attack somebody. The repeated line switches from 他, “he,” to 我们, “we,” so the violent hothead is no longer kept at a comfortable distance. The ending implicates the speakers in the volatility they describe. That pronoun change matters as much as the threatening vocabulary.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)

About Jackzebra and this mixtape

Zhuang Zhuang Mixtape arrived on Surf Gang on October 2, 2026: 55 tracks, opening with Sour and closing with Sweet. Its cast widens from YoungQueenz on Poker Face to User116, Effie, kuru, yoyi, 春 and 南部犯罪份子. Aghast has a production credit on every track from Hitman through Snatch, giving that stretch a shared collaborator behind its changing scenes.

Surf Gang release · Artist credits

Jackzebra told AVYSS that he writes while singing over a beat he has listened to repeatedly, keeping the images in his head central. He values the room Mandarin leaves for indirect meanings. Listen for ordinary phrases becoming physical scenes: familiarity becomes cooking, authority becomes family seniority, and a tired saying suddenly turns into a threat.

AVYSS interview, 2024

In STATIC, he describes mixtapes as a format for letting ideas flow, reserving an official debut album for later. In a separate conversation about Above & Beyond, he compared that earlier tape to a collection of his producer friends’ work. The credits here likewise reward attention: long-running collaborators sit alongside guests working in Mandarin, Korean and English.

STATIC interview · Sabukaru interview, 2025

The small details connect to his stated interests: he has described playing Temple Run in transit and before shows, watching Top Boy, and wanting to score White Oleander. These give the songs specific points of contact with his life. The notes follow those connections alongside the lyrics’ jokes, invented scenes and competing voices.

His recommendations in Perfectly Imperfect · Dazed interview, 2025 · Interview questionnaire, 2025

Jackzebra has pushed back on being made to represent all of China’s underground. These notes stay close to the words: what an expression usually means, what changes in this line, and how another song answers it. Cultural references have sources; interpretations rest on details you can hear or read in the song.
